components.text: Whether sufficiently grave pre-invasion conditions supplied a justification capable of overcoming the asserted presumption and forecast against war.
Whether experience of failed benevolent wars defeats confidence in this intervention's expected justification and outcome.
Whether sufficiently grave Iraqi conduct supplied concrete grounds capable of overcoming the presumption against a foreseeably disastrous war.
Whether this proposed intervention had grounds stronger than benevolent intention alone.
Whether intervention undertaken for benevolent reasons can be shown to have produced concrete good outcomes rather than merely intended benefits.
Whether the intervention's results were wholly disastrous in civilian, political, and strategic terms.
Whether the intervention produced concrete good outcomes rather than merely expressing benevolent intentions.
Whether actual post-removal gains undermine the forecast that the venture could yield only disaster.
Whether the enumerated postwar gains establish a defensible intervention once financial, human, strategic, institutional, and moral costs are included.
Whether the regime's atrocities and ambitions were sufficient to justify invasion under a coherent, consistently applied intervention principle.
Whether the claimed gains remain sufficient once financial, civilian, strategic, institutional, and moral costs are included.
Whether grave conduct by Saddam supplied a coherent and consistently applied justification for invasion.
Whether the intervention produced security consequences that materially offset the asserted strategic costs and weakened nonproliferation position.
Whether this intervention produced concrete beneficial effects sufficient to weaken general pessimism about benevolent wars.
Whether positive nonproliferation consequences answer the forecast that the intervention would end in overall disaster.
Whether the intervention generated security benefits capable of offsetting the asserted strategic and geopolitical costs.
Whether coercive intervention can produce identifiable beneficial consequences beyond good intentions.
Whether regional nonproliferation effects complicate the claim of foreseeable comprehensive disaster.
Whether initiating war was unjustified aggression or could follow from a principled forfeiture of sovereign protection by Iraq.
Whether humanitarian intervention rests on a coherent and consistently applicable doctrine rather than selective assertion.
Whether past intervention failures undermine confidence in the practical outcome of applying the forfeiture principle.
Whether there is a principled threshold capable of authorizing intervention despite the presumption against aggressive war.
Whether humanitarian intervention rests on a coherent principle rather than selective application.
Whether Iraq presented exceptional grounds beyond generic benevolent war-making.
Whether human moral capacities and solidarity can supply binding reasons for obedience without an authority beyond human preference.
Whether human solidarity and naturalistic self-understanding can create binding reasons for moral obedience without transcendent authority.
Whether transcendent authority is necessary to ground objective duties and provide binding reasons for moral obedience.
Whether transcendent religious authority supplies a morally defensible account of responsibility rather than displacing personal accountability.
Whether atonement necessarily removes personal guilt and responsibility, or instead redirects destructive impulses and offers hope under intolerable guilt.
Whether religious doctrines necessarily deny autonomous moral agency rather than redirect preexisting human impulses.
Whether sacrifice and atonement necessarily erase responsibility or can instead redirect destructive impulses and offer morally necessary hope.
Whether religious narrative can perform a constructive moral function rather than merely obstruct mature judgment.
Whether the Abraham narrative and divine authorization restrain destructive impulses or instead model unconditional submission capable of licensing cruelty.
Whether placing God above human judgment cures nihilism and supplies reliable moral restraint.
Whether Abrahamic sacrifice narratives redirect violence or instead model obedience willing to commit cruelty under claimed divine authority.
Whether invoking God reliably restrains nihilism and supplies morally superior binding authority.
Whether evolved solidarity and reciprocal self-interest explain objective rightness and supply reasons to obey when morality conflicts with personal advantage.
Whether autonomous human moral capacities can ground obligation independently of inherited religious morality.
Whether reciprocal self-interest explains objective rightness and supplies reasons to obey when doing right conflicts with personal advantage.
Whether possessing autonomous moral capacities is sufficient to ground binding moral obligation.
Whether genocide, proliferation violations, terrorism, and aggression can make intervention a justified exception to sovereign protection.
Whether Saddam's atrocities, aggression, and ambitions supplied sufficiently compelling grounds for forcible removal.
Whether identified grounds for sovereignty forfeiture erase the moral distinction between initiating war and declining intervention.
Whether regime brutality alone makes military action morally equivalent to inaction.
Whether improved natural explanations have resolved the relevant mysteries sufficiently to exclude skeptical discussion of intelligent design.
Whether improved natural explanations have resolved origins sufficiently to justify dismissing supernatural or design-oriented discussion.
Whether examples of cruelty committed under asserted divine permission establish that religious belief is predominantly corrupting or uniquely dangerous.
Whether a specific objection to atonement supports an overall negative moral assessment of religion.
Whether religion generally obstructs mature moral autonomy and civilizational progress.
Whether religiously authorized cruelty establishes that religion is on balance more harmful than morally constructive.
Whether religion generally obstructs moral progress and threatens human autonomy.
Whether religious belief contributes moral goods unavailable in the pro account's negative comparison.
Whether historical violence supports attributing superior net moral effects to religion and civilizational danger to unbelief.
Whether secular moral insufficiency is evidenced by twentieth-century totalitarian violence.
Whether atheism itself supplies permission for unrestricted conduct and political brutality.
Whether twentieth-century totalitarian atrocities establish a causal indictment of secular humanism or an aggregate advantage for religion.
Whether unbelief predictably removes restraints and thereby causes totalitarian violence.
Whether religious institutional resemblance defeats the claim that regimes expressly hostile to religion exemplify distinctively atheistic state violence.
Whether secular moral sufficiency is tested by revolutionary and state persecution undertaken under explicit unbelief.
Whether explicit antireligious ideology and persecution remain causally relevant despite totalitarian borrowing of religious forms.
